title: Cross v. United States (1964)
summary: Summary judgment may not be granted when the decisive facts turn on a party's motive or intent and rest on the credibility of the movant's own witness, because those inferences belong to the trier of fact after cross-examination at trial.
notes: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, 1964. Key line: "Summary judgment is particularly inappropriate where 'the inferences which the parties seek to have drawn deal with questions of motive, intent and subjective feelings and reactions.'" (Judge Moore, quoting Empire Electronics)

sections.Parties: Plaintiffs-appellees were Professor Ephraim Cross and his wife, who filed a joint federal income tax return for 1954. Cross was an Assistant Professor at City College in New York, where he taught French, Spanish and romance linguistics, the study of how Latin developed into the romance languages and their dialects. The Crosses sued for a refund after claiming a $1,300 deduction for the professor's summer travel. Defendant-appellant was the United States, represented by the United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York. The Government denied that the trip was a deductible business expense and appealed the grant of summary judgment. The appeal was argued before Circuit Judges Moore, Kaufman and Marshall, and Judge Moore wrote the opinion.
sections.Material Facts: On June 30, 1954, Cross, his wife and their pet dog sailed from New York on a French freighter. The ship called briefly at seven Mediterranean ports. Twenty-one days out, at Marseilles, they separated: Mrs. Cross toured with a friend, and the professor and the dog went to Paris. Cross pursued no formal study or research. He visited schools, courts, churches, book publishers, theaters, movies and cafes, read newspapers, heard radio, talked with students and teachers and attended political meetings. He returned on September 23, 1954. In a discovery deposition, taken without cross-examination, he said the trip's purpose was to maintain and improve his skill as a linguist and teacher. Section 162(a) allows ordinary and necessary business expenses; Treasury Regulation 1.162-5 permits education expenses that maintain job skills but treats travel as education as primarily personal. The Government called the trip a vacation, disputed the amount, and asked how much was spent on Mrs. Cross.
sections.Procedural History: The Crosses brought a refund suit in the Southern District of New York and moved for summary judgment. In support they filed affidavits from several professors saying foreign travel is desirable for a language teacher, together with the professor's pretrial deposition. The Government opposed the motion, asserting a right to cross-examine the Crosses at trial about the nature of their expenses and the educational benefits sought, and to cross-examine the affiant professors. The district court held there was no genuine issue of material fact and granted the motion, reasoning that the Government had produced no facts refuting the professor's stated purpose and had already had a chance to cross-examine him at the deposition. Cross v. United States, 222 F. Supp. 157 (S.D.N.Y. 1963). The Government appealed. The Second Circuit heard argument on June 1, 1964, and on August 7, 1964, reversed and remanded for trial.
sections.Issue: The only question on appeal was whether there were triable issues of fact that made the grant of summary judgment erroneous under Rule 56(c). More specifically, when the dispositive question is the taxpayer's primary purpose in traveling, the relevant facts lie largely within his own knowledge, and the only evidence of purpose is his own deposition testimony and supporting affidavits, may a court decide the case on the papers because the opposing party has offered no contrary evidence, or must the case go to trial so that the trier of fact can weigh credibility after cross-examination? The court also had to consider whether the amounts attributable to educational purpose, to Mrs. Cross and to the preliminary voyage presented separate questions of fact.
sections.Holding: Summary judgment was improvidently granted, and the Government is entitled to a trial at which all the circumstances can be developed for the trier of fact. Whether expenses are ordinary and necessary in carrying on a trade or business is essentially a factual question, and here the ultimate facts were warmly contested. Because many facts remained within the professor's own knowledge, the Government had to be allowed to test his credibility on cross-examination. Summary judgment is particularly inappropriate where the inferences sought concern motive, intent and subjective feelings, and a judge may not draw fact inferences on such a motion. The rule that bare pleadings cannot defeat a supported motion does not justify summary relief where the disputed facts turn exclusively on the credibility of the movant's witnesses. The judgment was reversed and the case remanded for trial.
sections.Reasoning: Rule 56(c) permits summary judgment only where there is no genuine issue as to any material fact, and the ordinary-and-necessary inquiry rarely fits that description. A factfinder must decide what parts of a trip, if any, are vacation and what parts are education. Nobody disputed that Cross taught languages and went abroad, but the facts about purpose were his alone, and the Government was entitled to probe them before the trier of fact. Quoting Empire Electronics and Bragen, the court stressed that inferences about motive and intent may be drawn only at trial. Dressler's rule that pleadings alone cannot resist a supported motion does not apply when everything rests on the credibility of the movant's own witnesses. Revenue Ruling 64-176 confirms the point: a French teacher who travels through France may deduct the cost only if he shows that his itinerary and the major portion of his activities were undertaken primarily to improve his skills. A trial lawyer who visits the Old Bailey does not thereby deduct his whole vacation. The trier of fact must also allocate amounts: the twenty-one days before Marseilles, Mrs. Cross's share, and the dog's charges. Finally, discovery depositions do not replace the right to call and examine the adverse party before the jury, as Arnstein v. Porter held.

topics.cp-summary-judgment: Rule 56(c) allows judgment only where no genuine issue of material fact exists, and a contested question of a taxpayer's primary purpose is not such a case.
topics.cp-inferences: Inferences about motive, intent and subjective feelings may be drawn only at trial, and the credibility of the movant's own witness is for the trier of fact after cross-examination.
topics.cp-judge-jury: A judge ruling on a summary judgment motion may not draw fact inferences or weigh credibility; those tasks belong to the jury or other trier of fact.
topics.cp-burden-production: The rule that bare pleadings cannot defeat a supported motion does not shift the burden to the nonmovant when the movant's showing rests entirely on the credibility of his own witnesses.
topics.cp-frcp-56: The case reads the 1964 text of Rule 56(c) and shows the pre-Celotex reluctance to resolve state-of-mind questions on the papers.

learning.separateOpinions: None. Judge Moore wrote for a unanimous panel that also included Judges Kaufman and Marshall. The opinion carries one footnote noting the founding in May 1961 of the Association for a World Language, which sought to teach every schoolchild a second language, offered in support of the court's remark that the enlightened teaching of modern languages aids international understanding.
learning.why: Cross is the standard illustration of why summary judgment is disfavored when the material fact is a state of mind and the proof lies in the credibility of the movant's own witness: a judge may not weigh credibility or draw inferences on the papers, and discovery depositions do not substitute for cross-examination before the trier of fact. It frames the later shift in Celotex and its companions toward a more demanding burden on the nonmovant.
